questions.q: When does .distinct() consider two rows duplicates?
options: Only when every single column matches exactly between the two rows
Only when the first column matches
When any one column matches between the two rows
.distinct() never removes any rows regardless of content
questions.explain: Even a stray whitespace difference in one column, like Lesson 49 would have caught, counts them as different rows.

questions.q: How does dropDuplicates(["Zone"]) differ from distinct()?
options: It requires every column to match, just like distinct()
It's exactly identical to distinct() in every case
It treats two rows as duplicates if they match on just the named column(s), ignoring every other column completely
It only works on numeric columns
questions.explain: This is usually what you actually want in practice — matching duplicate identity on a specific set of columns.

questions.q: When dropDuplicates() finds multiple matching rows, which one does it keep?
options: Always the row with the most recent timestamp
It keeps all of them and only removes exact full-row duplicates
Always the first row encountered in the file
An arbitrary one — there's no guaranteed 'keep the first' or 'keep the most recent' rule
questions.explain: If which specific row survives actually matters, sort first and use Window functions (Lesson 57) instead.

questions.q: Why does 'duplicate' always need a definition before removing rows?
options: There is only ever one correct definition of duplicate, in every case
Because two rows can be duplicates by one definition (like matching trip identity) but not another (like matching on every single column)
Because PySpark has no built-in concept of duplicates at all
Because duplicates only exist in CSV files, never Parquet
questions.explain: A trip re-ingested with a corrected fare_amount is a 'duplicate' by trip identity, but not by distinct()'s all-columns rule.

questions.q: Why might trips.dropDuplicates(["VendorID", "tpep_pickup_datetime", "tpep_dropoff_datetime"]) catch a duplicate that .distinct() misses?
options: Because the two copies might differ slightly in another column, like a recalculated fare_amount, which distinct() would treat as making them different rows
dropDuplicates() always returns more rows than distinct(), regardless of the data
There is no real difference between the two in this scenario
distinct() is stricter and always removes strictly more rows than dropDuplicates()
questions.explain: distinct() requires every column to match; dropDuplicates() with a subset ignores columns not in that subset.
